title: Venture capital and private equity, from the beginning
audience: A curious reader coming from a different field. You do not need a finance background or experience running a company.
scope: An introduction to investing in businesses through venture, growth, and buyout funds, with software companies as everyday examples. It explains common arrangements rather than any particular investment firm's terms. Fund structures, investor access, and ownership rights vary by country and agreement. The people, businesses, and financial examples are fictional.
learningGoals: Explain how venture capital and buyouts help with different business needs.
Identify whose money is involved, who makes decisions, and who receives the money.
Follow an investment from fundraising to company ownership and an eventual sale.
Distinguish business progress, an estimated investment value, and money actually returned.
Recognize the main tensions around growth, control, debt, and timing.

introduction.whatItIs:
Imagine Maya has built software that helps repair businesses schedule their workers. Customers like it, but hiring a sales team costs money before those extra sales arrive. Elsewhere, an owner of an established software business wants to retire. These are different problems, yet both might be solved by bringing in a new business owner.

Venture capital and private equity involve investing money in return for a share of business ownership. Here, private generally means the ownership is not freely traded on a stock exchange. Investors hope their ownership becomes more valuable and can eventually be sold. They can also lose money. The work combines choosing businesses, agreeing on ownership, helping or overseeing them, and finding a way to return money to investors.
introduction.whyItMatters: The effects reach beyond investors: companies may gain resources to grow, founders may sell part of what they built, and employees and customers may experience changes in priorities. Understanding the domain means following both the money and the decisions it enables.
introduction.familiarComparison: Think of several people contributing money to help someone expand a neighborhood business. They appoint a representative to examine the plan, negotiate their share, and stay involved. The investors share the potential rewards and risks.
introduction.whereComparisonBreaks: Professional investing separates the investors, the investment organization, and the businesses they own. Detailed agreements govern their relationship. Investors may have to wait many years to get money back, and owning shares does not automatically mean running the business every day.

participants.name: The fund investors
participants.role: Organizations such as pension funds, or other eligible investors, pool money in a fund: an arrangement for investing together. In a partnership structure, these investors are called limited partners, shortened to LPs.
participants.caresAbout: Returns after costs, the possibility of losses, trustworthy reporting, and when money may come back.

participants.name: The investment manager
participants.role: Selects investments and oversees them for the fund. You may hear the managing side called the general partner, or GP; precise legal roles depend on the structure.
participants.caresAbout: Finding worthwhile investments, supporting them, earning fees and a possible share of profits, and retaining investors' confidence.

participants.name: Founders, selling owners, and company management
participants.role: Founders may seek money for growth or sell ownership. Management runs the business. These can be the same people, but they need not be.
participants.caresAbout: Resources, an acceptable price, decision-making freedom, and a workable relationship after the agreement is signed.

participants.name: Lenders and specialist advisers
participants.role: Lenders may supply borrowed money. Lawyers, accountants, and other specialists help examine and complete investments; fund administrators maintain records and reporting.
participants.caresAbout: For lenders, repayment. For advisers and administrators, accurate work within their responsibilities. Neither role is the same as owning the business.

participants.name: Employees and customers
participants.role: Keep the business working and buying its services, although they may have little say in an ownership transaction.
participants.caresAbout: Good jobs, dependable products, fair treatment, and continuity when ownership or strategy changes.

concepts.term: Venture capital, growth investment, and buyouts
concepts.meaning:
A venture is a risky or uncertain project or business. Venture capital (VC) invests in young companies with high growth potential but also significant uncertainty. Growth investing supports more established companies that want to expand, while buyouts involve acquiring control of an existing business. These categories can overlap.

Private equity (PE) is a broad term that includes venture capital. However, in everyday industry use, PE often refers more specifically to buyout investing.
concepts.example: Funding Maya to prove a young business model is a venture case. Funding expansion after it is established may be a growth case. Buying control from an owner who wants to leave is a buyout case.
concepts.whyItMatters: Different needs call for different investors, expectations, and ownership arrangements. A company does not have to pass through all three stages.
concepts.illustrationPrompt: Three independent, equally sized panels, with no arrows or timeline between them. Left: a small software team testing a prototype on a laptop, an investor listening; label "Venture" and "Prove an idea". Middle: an established software team expanding into an additional office, a manager and investor reviewing the expansion; label "Growth" and "Expand a business". Right: an existing business owner handing a symbolic key to a new controlling owner, while the business and employees continue; label "Buyout" and "Change control". These are alternative investment situations, not a required sequence. Avoid plants, rockets, ladders, or success charts.

media.title: Venture capital, growth investment, and buyouts
media.alt: Three separate scenes: a team tests a software prototype, an established business expands, and an owner hands a key to a new controlling owner.
media.caption: Venture funding, growth investment, and buyouts meet different needs. They are not compulsory stages in a company’s life.

concepts.term: The firm, the fund, and the portfolio
concepts.meaning: The firm is the investment organization. A fund is a separate arrangement that pools investors' money under agreed rules. The portfolio is the set of investments it holds.
concepts.example: One firm may manage several funds raised at different times. Each fund has its own investors, commitments, and investments.
concepts.whyItMatters: Money raised for a fund is not sales revenue earned by the investment firm.
concepts.illustrationPrompt: Draw one investment office with two people at the top, labeled "Investment firm". Beneath it, two separate large containers labeled "Fund A" and "Fund B". A connector from the investment firm to each fund is labeled "Manages". Within each fund container, place two small generic company office buildings, each with a person visible at a window, grouped under the label "Portfolio". These are companies, not products or market sectors. The complete allowed text in this picture is: "Investment firm", "Manages", "Fund A", "Fund B", "Portfolio", and "Company". Label each small office "Company". Use no acronyms, industry names, product names, software symbols, or other text. Keep the firm clearly outside the fund containers, and each portfolio inside its own fund. No money arrows or mixing funds.

media.title: The firm, the fund, and the portfolio
media.alt: One investment firm manages two separate funds. Each fund contains its own portfolio of companies.
media.caption: The firm manages the funds; each fund holds a portfolio of investments. The arrows show management relationships, not money transfers.

concepts.term: A commitment and a capital call
concepts.meaning: A commitment is an investor's promise to provide an agreed amount. A capital call is a request to pay part of that commitment when the fund needs it, under its agreement.
concepts.example: An investor commits €10 million. A €2 million call asks for part of that amount now; it does not mean the entire €10 million has already been spent.
concepts.whyItMatters: A promise of money, cash received, and cash invested are different things. Calls can also fund agreed fees and expenses.
concepts.illustrationPrompt: Three spacious panels for one illustrative example: "Promise", "Request", "Payment". Promise: an investor signs a commitment document reading "€10m committed". Request: the fund manager sends that investor a notice reading "€2m called"; use a paper notice, not cash, here. Payment: the investor transfers money to the fund, with a clear single arrow from investor to fund and label "€2m paid". The investor and fund remain recognizable across panels. Only the payment panel contains moving money. Do not show €10m paid or invested, or any subsequent company investment.

media.title: A commitment and a capital call
media.alt: An investor signs a €10 million commitment, receives a €2 million capital call, and then pays €2 million to the fund.
media.caption: In this illustrative case, the investor pays the amount called. A €10 million commitment does not mean €10 million has already been paid or invested.

concepts.meaning: Equity means ownership. Debt means borrowed money with repayment obligations. Equity owners receive what remains for them after obligations are met; lenders have different rights.
concepts.example: A fund might buy shares using investors' money while a lender also finances the acquisition. Using borrowing to support a purchase is called leverage.
concepts.whyItMatters: Debt can magnify both gains and losses for owners. Loan payments can strain a business even when its long-term idea is promising. Not every investment uses debt.
concepts.illustrationPrompt: Two clearly separated panels, labeled "Equity" and "Debt". Equity: an investor provides money to a business and holds a share certificate showing a simple ownership symbol, with label "Ownership". Debt: a lender supplies a loan to a business; a blue arrow from lender to business is labeled "Loan", and a separate amber arrow back to lender is labeled "Repayment". Clearly point the arrowheads in opposite directions. Give the business and lender recognizable buildings or people. No percentages, profit chart, guaranteed returns, or suggestion that a loan grants ordinary ownership.

media.title: Equity and debt
media.alt: An equity investor exchanges money for ownership. A lender provides a loan, with repayment flowing in the opposite direction.
media.caption: Ownership and a repayment obligation give investors and lenders different rights. The picture shows the basic distinction, not a promise of profit or repayment.

concepts.meaning: When a company issues new shares, the payment goes to the company. When an owner sells existing shares, the payment goes to that seller. A transaction can combine both.
concepts.example: Maya's business can receive money to hire people, or Maya can personally receive money for selling ownership. Those are different uses of an investment.
concepts.whyItMatters: A headline saying a company received investment does not tell you how much cash entered its bank account.
concepts.illustrationPrompt: Draw two equally sized comparison panels with simple people and company buildings. Panel 1 title: "New shares". A person labeled "Buyer" stands at the left. A company building labeled "Company" stands at the right. Draw ONE cash arrow from Buyer to Company, decorated with a few banknotes. The caption "Company receives money" appears ONCE below this entire panel. The buyer holds a share certificate, but do not draw an arrow for shares. Panel 2 title: "Existing shares". A person labeled "Buyer" stands at the left. A selling owner labeled "Seller" stands at the right. Draw ONE cash arrow from Buyer to Seller, decorated with a few banknotes. Show the company in a smaller background position, separate from that cash route. The caption "Seller receives money" appears ONCE below this entire panel. The buyer holds an existing share certificate, but do not draw an arrow for shares. There are exactly TWO arrows in the whole illustration, one cash arrow per panel, both pointing left to right. Do not repeat captions anywhere or add any other labels. The lesson is who receives the purchase money.

media.title: New shares versus existing shares
media.alt: For new shares, the buyer pays the company. For existing shares, the buyer pays the selling owner while the company stays outside that cash route.
media.caption: Follow the money: newly issued shares fund the company; a sale of existing shares pays the seller.

concepts.meaning: Dilution is a reduction in an existing owner's percentage when new shares are issued. Control concerns who can make which decisions; it depends on voting rights and agreements as well as percentages.
concepts.example: Maya may own a smaller percentage after raising money while still leading the company. A minority investor may nevertheless have approval rights over particular major decisions.
concepts.whyItMatters: The price, the ownership percentage, and the decision rights all matter when comparing offers.
concepts.illustrationPrompt: Two distinct panels: "Ownership percentage" and "Decision rights". The left panel uses a clearly illustrative arithmetic example. Show two simple large text badges side by side: a badge headed "Before" containing exactly "You: 4 shares", "Total: 8 shares", and "50%"; a badge headed "After" containing exactly "You: 4 shares", "Total: 10 shares", and "40%". An arrow points from Before to After, with the short label "New shares issued". A friendly founder below holds the same folder labeled "4 shares". Under this panel, place "Same shares, smaller percentage". Do not draw counted tiles, pie charts, grids, dots, or other shapes suggesting quantities; use the exact numerical labels. The calculation is 4/8 = 50% before and 4/10 = 40% after. In the right panel, show that founder leading a small meeting while an investor refers to a written agreement. Below it place "Check the agreement". No arrow joins the ownership panel to the decision-rights panel. Make all requested text large and legible and add no extra text. The numerical example is invented to explain dilution, not a market statistic.

media.title: Dilution and control
media.alt: An illustrative holding of four shares falls from 50% of eight total shares to 40% of ten. Separately, a founder leads a meeting while an investor checks their agreement.
media.caption: Illustrative numbers: four shares out of eight is 50%; four out of ten is 40%. Decision rights also depend on voting arrangements and agreements.

concepts.term: Valuation, an exit, and a distribution
concepts.meaning: A valuation estimates what an investment is worth. An exit means selling some or all of it, for example to another company or investor. A distribution transfers money or other proceeds from the fund to its investors.
concepts.example: A report can show Maya's company gaining value without anyone receiving cash. A later sale may realize that value, a different value, or a loss.
concepts.whyItMatters: An estimated gain is not spendable cash. Listing shares on a stock exchange also does not necessarily let every investor sell immediately.
concepts.illustrationPrompt: Three distinct panels, labeled "Estimate", "Sell", and "Distribute". Estimate: a company beside an appraisal report, with label "Value on paper" and no cash. Sell: a buyer acquires a company investment from a fund and pays the fund; depict the payment clearly entering the fund, with label "Sale proceeds". Distribute: that fund sends a portion of proceeds to its investors, with label "Paid to investors". Use recognizable company, fund, buyer, and investor symbols with ample spacing. Do not draw money moving directly from the report to investors, rising price charts, equal sized money piles implying no fees, or guaranteed gains. This illustrates the distinction between three events; estimates do not guarantee that a sale or payment will occur.

media.title: Valuation, an exit, and a distribution
media.alt: Three panels distinguish a valuation report, a buyer paying sale proceeds to a fund, and the fund distributing proceeds to investors.
media.caption: A value on paper, a completed sale, and a payment to investors are different events. A valuation does not guarantee either a sale or a distribution.

historyNote: These selected US and European milestones explain parts of today's industry. They are not a claim that business investment began at one moment or followed the same path everywhere.

history.change: American Research and Development Corporation was established in the United States, with Georges Doriot as its president. It was one of the early modern venture investment organizations.
history.whyItMatters: It illustrates the move toward an organized combination of outside money, investment judgment, and support for new businesses.

history.period: The 1980s: the rise of debt-financed buyouts
history.change: A major US buyout wave used substantial borrowing to acquire established companies. Research on this period examines both the financial structure and changes in ownership and management.
history.whyItMatters: This history helps explain why discussion of private equity often centers on control, company performance, and the pressure created by debt.

history.period: 1994 onward: public institutions support European finance
history.change: The European Investment Fund was established in 1994. Its role includes working with financial partners to improve businesses' access to finance, including investment capital.
history.whyItMatters: Private business investment can involve public institutions alongside private investors. Different participants may combine commercial return goals with broader economic aims.

walkthrough.title: Maya's software business: raising money or selling ownership
walkthrough.setup: Maya and her company, ShiftPlan, are fictional. Follow a young-company investment, then compare it with an alternative buyout situation. The euro amounts teach the mechanics; they are not market prices or return forecasts. The ownership arithmetic assumes all shares have the same rights, and nobody else holds shares or rights to obtain them.

steps.title: Investors choose a fund and its purpose
steps.whatHappens: Before investing in ShiftPlan, a manager raises a fund with an agreed strategy: what kinds of companies it may back and how it will operate. Investors examine the team, terms, and track record before committing money.
steps.whyItMatters: The manager is investing other people's money within an agreement. A venture strategy and a buyout strategy may belong in different funds.

steps.title: Maya and the investor examine each other
steps.whatHappens: Maya explains what the extra money would help achieve. The venture investor checks customers, finances, technology, and the team. This investigation is called due diligence. Maya also asks other founders what the investor is like when a company struggles.
steps.whyItMatters: Both sides are choosing a relationship that may last years.
steps.watchOut: A promising sales forecast may depend heavily on one customer renewing. The parties need to understand that dependency before treating the forecast as dependable.

steps.title: Agree on the price and rights
steps.whatHappens: They agree to value the existing ownership at €8 million before the investment. The fund will put €2 million into newly issued shares. In this simplified case, the ownership value immediately after investment is €10 million: the fund owns 20% and Maya owns 80%.
steps.whyItMatters: Maya now owns a smaller percentage of a business with more resources. Separately, the agreement determines board seats and approval rights. A board oversees major company decisions.

steps.title: Complete the investment and follow the cash
steps.whatHappens: Required approvals and documents are completed, and the fund arranges its cash, calling investor commitments as needed. The €2 million goes into ShiftPlan's bank account because this is a new-share investment. Maya receives no personal sale proceeds in this version.
steps.whyItMatters: Fundraising by a fund, investment into a company, and payment to a founder are separate transactions.
steps.watchOut: Compare an alternative mature-business case: a buyout fund pays Maya €8 million for 80% of her existing shares. That payment goes to Maya, and ShiftPlan receives none of it. Extra company funding would need a separate arrangement.

steps.title: Work on the business and face setbacks
steps.whatHappens: ShiftPlan hires carefully and tests a new sales approach. Maya's team still runs the company; investors may help with recruitment, introductions, and major decisions. Management reports progress and cash needs.
steps.whyItMatters: The investment agreement starts the ownership period; it does not deliver business improvement by itself.
steps.watchOut: Sales take longer than expected. The team revises spending and milestones. The fund considers whether further investment is justified; another round of funding is not automatic.

steps.title: Sell an investment and return proceeds
steps.whatHappens: Imagine a successful later sale of all ShiftPlan's shares for €15 million. If the fund still owns 20%, rights are equal, and no other claims or costs intervene, its share is €3 million. Against its €2 million investment, that is a €1 million gain before costs. The fund then handles proceeds under its agreement, including any distributions.
steps.whyItMatters: The company sale price, the fund's proceeds, its gain, and the investors' final receipts are different amounts.
steps.watchOut: The sale could happen later, at a lower price, or never. Later funding could also change the ownership percentages or payment rights. If the business fails with nothing left for shareholders, the equity investment can be lost.

walkthrough.outcome: The venture case gave ShiftPlan resources to grow; the buyout comparison gave an existing owner a way to sell. The investor's result depends on the price paid, business performance, ownership terms, costs, and eventual proceeds. A signed deal is only the beginning.
walkthrough.illustrationPrompt:
Create a sparse, spacious story in six panels: two rows of three, read left to right. Each panel has ONE simple scene, at most three people, and at most two relevant objects. Preserve the same Maya throughout: an adult woman with medium-brown skin, shoulder-length dark curly hair, a teal jacket, and dark trousers. The investment manager is a different person, in blue.
Panel 1: investors and a manager sit together with one plain folder, agreeing on their fund’s purpose. Heading: "1 Choose a fund".
Panel 2: Maya and the manager face one another, each holding one plain folder and asking questions. Heading: "2 Check each other".
Panel 3: Maya and the manager sign one agreement at a small desk. Heading: "3 Agree the terms".
Panel 4: a simple container labeled "Fund" sends a single arrow with banknotes into a company office labeled "ShiftPlan". Maya stands outside the arrow. Heading: "4 Invest in the company".
Panel 5: Maya and two colleagues adjust their plan at a desk, with a calendar and a simple blank checklist. Heading: "5 Work and adapt". One short caption: "Sales take longer".
Panel 6: Maya, the manager, and a potential buyer discuss a possible sale at a desk with a clock. Heading: "6 Possible sale". One short caption: "A sale is not guaranteed".
CRITICAL TEXT LIMIT: The headings, Fund, ShiftPlan, Sales take longer, and A sale is not guaranteed are the ONLY text allowed anywhere. Do not write on the folders, documents, calendar, checklist, screens, background, or clothing. Use a few plain strokes on paper without letters. No thought bubbles, speech bubbles, charts, dashboards, tables, logos, industry icons, extra symbols, statistics, prices, percentages, acronyms, explanations, or financial vocabulary. The surrounding prose explains every detail; this image only helps readers remember the six stages. Use large headings, broad empty margins, and simple recognizable actions. Keep the atmosphere professional and suitable for adults, with restrained flat color. Do not blend the alternative buyout case into this venture story.

media.title: Maya's software business: raising money or selling ownership
media.alt: Six scenes follow Maya’s fictional investment: choosing a fund, examining each other, agreeing terms, paying money into ShiftPlan, adjusting spending after slower sales, and considering a possible sale.
media.caption: The investment gives ShiftPlan resources to grow. Its people still need to adapt when plans meet reality, and a later sale and return of proceeds are not guaranteed.

valueAndIncentives.title: Business improvement and investor returns are related, but different
valueAndIncentives.explanation: Better products, stronger customer relationships, or more effective operations may make a company more valuable. Investors' returns also depend on the purchase price, borrowing, and what a future buyer will pay. Growth alone does not settle the calculation.
valueAndIncentives.example: ShiftPlan can win more customers yet disappoint its investors if the initial price assumed much faster growth. Conversely, a financial gain does not by itself prove better outcomes for employees or customers.

valueAndIncentives.title: The manager is paid separately from the companies it owns
valueAndIncentives.explanation: A management fee pays for investment management. Carried interest, often called carry, is an agreed share of investment profits. Eligibility, calculation, and payment order depend on the fund agreement. Neither is simply the revenue of a portfolio company.
valueAndIncentives.example: ShiftPlan earns revenue by selling software. A fund may later earn a gain by selling its shares. The manager's fee and possible profit share are another layer, and they affect what fund investors ultimately receive.

valueAndIncentives.title: Useful success measures follow the whole journey
valueAndIncentives.explanation: At company level, ask whether customers stay, the business generates or consumes cash, and its plans are working. At fund level, distinguish cash already returned from the estimated value of unsold holdings, and account for time and costs.
valueAndIncentives.example: A fund reporting a large estimated gain is in a different position from one that has already returned the same amount in cash. Neither number alone tells the whole story.

challenges.title: Choosing under uncertainty
challenges.whyHard: Investors must decide before they know how a company will perform. Founders usually know more about their business, while investors may see patterns across several businesses.
challenges.tradeOff: Waiting for more certainty can mean missing an opportunity; acting quickly can mean buying an attractive story with weak foundations.
challenges.example: ShiftPlan's enthusiastic early customers may not represent a much larger market.
challenges.commonApproach: Check underlying assumptions, speak with customers, and identify what would change the decision. Investigation reduces avoidable mistakes; it cannot remove uncertainty.

challenges.title: Growing while keeping enough cash
challenges.whyHard: Hiring and product development use money before their benefits arrive. Young businesses may need another investment before they can fund themselves.
challenges.tradeOff: Spending faster can accelerate learning and growth, but leaves less time to recover from setbacks.
challenges.example: ShiftPlan hires its full planned sales team before discovering which sales approach works.
challenges.commonApproach: Stage spending against meaningful progress and revisit how long available cash will last. Reserve money for follow-on investments where appropriate, while recognizing that neither investors nor companies have unlimited resources.

challenges.title: Using debt without making the business fragile
challenges.whyHard: A buyout financed partly with borrowing creates repayment and interest obligations. Weaker trading or more expensive borrowing can reduce the room to maneuver.
challenges.tradeOff: Borrowing reduces the initial ownership money needed, but can amplify losses and compete with spending on people and products.
challenges.example: An established ShiftPlan loses a major customer while acquisition-related loan payments still fall due.
challenges.commonApproach: Examine less favorable operating scenarios and preserve financial room for them. More conservative borrowing can help, but no financing structure makes a weak business automatically strong.

challenges.title: Agreeing whose priorities shape the company
challenges.whyHard: Founders, managers, fund investors, employees, and customers can want different things at different times. Ownership brings influence, but the consequences are shared more widely.
challenges.tradeOff: Closer oversight can improve discipline or undermine useful autonomy. Cost reductions can improve short-term figures while damaging service or employee trust.
challenges.example: Cutting support staff improves ShiftPlan's immediate costs, but slower responses cause customers to leave later.
challenges.commonApproach: Make decision rights clear, test the operating consequences of changes, and discuss conflicts openly. Aligned incentives and transparent reporting help; they do not eliminate disagreement.

challenges.title: Turning years of work into an actual return
challenges.whyHard: A good business may have no attractive buyer when the fund wants to sell. Many funds have an agreed lifetime, but the companies and markets follow their own schedules.
challenges.tradeOff: Selling now provides money sooner; waiting may improve the price or make the outcome worse.
challenges.example: ShiftPlan meets its operating goals just as potential buyers reduce their acquisition budgets.
challenges.commonApproach: Prepare credible sale information early, consider more than one route, and communicate uncertainty about timing. Report unsold investments as estimates, without presenting them as completed cash returns.

misconceptions.belief: VC and PE are two completely separate kinds of money.
misconceptions.reality: Venture capital belongs to the wider private-equity family. The everyday VC-versus-PE comparison usually means young-company investment versus buyouts, with growth investment in between.

misconceptions.belief: An investment announcement tells us how much money the company can spend.
misconceptions.reality: Some money may buy shares from existing owners. Follow the payment to distinguish company funding from seller proceeds.

misconceptions.belief: A larger valuation means investors have already made that money.
misconceptions.reality: The valuation is an estimate. Investors still need proceeds, and their receipts depend on ownership, obligations, costs, and the fund agreement.

misconceptions.belief: Every good business should seek venture capital.
misconceptions.reality: A healthy business can grow using customer income or other financing. Venture investing usually needs the possibility of substantial growth and an eventual investor return; that is not every owner's aim.

takeaways: Start with the business need: funding a young company, expanding an established one, or changing its ownership.
Keep the firm, fund, company, and individual owners separate when following money.
Price, ownership percentage, and decision rights tell different parts of an investment's story.
Business progress matters, but investor results also depend on costs, debt, sale conditions, and time.
An estimated value is not a distribution, and a completed investment is not a guaranteed success.

knowledgeChecks.question: A fund pays Maya €8 million for shares she already owns. How much of that payment can ShiftPlan use to hire people?
knowledgeChecks.answer: None automatically. The payment goes to Maya as the seller.
knowledgeChecks.explanation: The company needs its own funding arrangement to receive cash. Buying shares from an owner and paying the company for new shares have different recipients.

knowledgeChecks.question: An investor commits €10 million and has so far paid €2 million into the fund. Has the fund already received the full commitment?
knowledgeChecks.answer: No. It has received €2 million of that investor's commitment.
knowledgeChecks.explanation: The remaining commitment is a future funding obligation under the agreement, not cash already in the fund's bank account.

knowledgeChecks.question: ShiftPlan wins more customers, but its fund cannot find a buyer. Have those gains become cash returns for investors?
knowledgeChecks.answer: Not simply because the business improved or its estimated value rose.
knowledgeChecks.explanation: Business progress may support future value. Turning ownership into proceeds, and distributing them, are additional steps with their own uncertainties.

knowledgeChecks.question: Why might Maya reject the investor offering the highest headline valuation?
knowledgeChecks.answer: Its decision rights, expectations, or approach to setbacks might make it a poor partner.
knowledgeChecks.explanation: The relationship extends beyond the price. Ownership terms and practical support can affect how the business develops for years.

nextQuestions: What business need does this investment serve, and why is this fund suited to it?
Which money goes into the company, which goes to sellers, and what obligations accompany it?
Which decisions change hands after investment, and which remain with management?
What would make the investment case fail, and who would feel the effects?
How much reported value has actually been returned, and what remains uncertain?

Use a landscape canvas with the main line running left to right: a pair of people labeled "Fund investors", a clearly separate container labeled "Fund", and a company office labeled "Company". An arrow from Fund investors to Fund says "Provide money". A relationship connector from Fund to Company says "Holds shares"; do not decorate this connector with cash, because buying existing shares pays the seller. Above the Fund, put a person labeled "Investment manager" with a connector down to Fund labeled "Manages". Inside the Company office show a founder and colleague labeled "Founder and management", with the small phrase "Run the business". Keep them distinct from the fund manager. At the right, show an optional "Lender" with an arrow to Company labeled "May lend". Below the Fund, place two specialists labeled "Advisers"; connect them to Fund and Company with lines labeled "Checks and advice". These labels and relationships are the full teaching content of the image; use ample white space and large type.

media.title: The people involved
media.alt: Fund investors provide money to a fund managed by an investment manager. The fund holds company shares; founders and management run the company. Lenders may lend, advisers help with checks, employees work there, and customers buy its products.
media.caption: Read the labels on the connections: providing money, managing a fund, and holding company shares are different roles. Lenders may be involved; employees and customers experience the effects of company decisions.
